fatal_errors: The proposed material is single-phase CoCrFeMnNi rather than the as-cast FCC+B2 AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA.
The intervention is simultaneous high-temperature, high-strain-rate deformation rather than intermediate-temperature thermal aging.
The hypothesis omits the decisive non-monotonic ductile-brittle-ductile response, including minimum ductility near 600°C and recovery near 750°C.
Dynamic nanocrystalline grain refinement and grain-boundary decohesion replace the target mediators of enhanced L12 ordering and jagged FCC/B2 phase boundaries.
The cited evidence does not establish that elevated-temperature tensile loading dynamically creates 10–50 nm high-angle grains that cause segregation-free brittle fracture.
The experiment changes temperature and strain rate together, preventing attribution of any toughness loss to either variable.
explanation: The response addresses HEA embrittlement and gives a nominally falsifiable same-alloy comparison, but it reconstructs neither the material system nor the thermal-aging mechanism. The target concerns ordering and phase-boundary evolution in a dual-phase eutectic HEA, producing a bounded 550–750°C brittle window and subsequent ductility recovery. The generated hypothesis instead combines intermediate-temperature ductility-loss evidence with tribological severe-plastic-deformation and grain-boundary-energy observations to propose dynamic refinement and decohesion. E1 supports intermediate-temperature ductility loss only; E2 concerns localized sliding-induced refinement and friction; E3 offers a cautious suggestion of possible boundary decohesion but does not validate the claimed tensile-service pathway. The proposed microscopy and toughness measurements could test its own mechanism, but the design is confounded and would not test the ordering, jagged phase-boundary, dislocation-pile-up, or ductile-transition-zone predictions that distinguish the hidden target from conventional segregation embrittlement.
